en: The Jātaka:
The Collection of Twenty, Chapter on Mātaṅga.
2. The Citta-sambhūta Jātaka:
“Everything well-performed by men bears fruit;
there is nothing whatsoever that is in vain through karma.”
I see one who has come into being with great majesty,
endowed with the fruit of merit through his own karma;
for all well-performed deeds of men bear fruit.
There is nothing at all that is fruitless through action;
could it be that my mind is likewise, so that his willpower is as great as mine?
“Every well-performed deed of men bears fruit;
there is nothing whatsoever that is fruitless through karma.
Know the mind to be exactly the same, O Deva.”
“His mind is powerful, just like yours.
“Has Master Citta heard this from another,
or has someone told it to you?”
“The verses are well-sung; I have no doubt.
I give you a choice village and a hundred cows.
“But Citta, I have not heard this from anyone else.”
And this matter was foretold to me by the seer:
"Having gone, recite a verse to the king;
he, being pleased, might grant you a boon."
“Harness the royal chariot,
well-crafted with embroidered cushions;
bind the girths of the elephants.”
Put on your necklaces. Let the kettledrums, drums, and conchs be sounded,
and let the swift vehicles be harnessed.
"Today I shall go to that hermitage,
where I will see the seer sitting there.
"Truly, it was a great gain for me!"
A well-sung verse in the midst of an assembly;
having seen the seer endowed with virtue and conduct,
I am thrilled and my mind is joyful.
“May your lordship accept from us a seat, water, and foot-washing water;
we ask your lordship’s consent regarding the guest-offering.”
“May your honor do us the highest honor.
“Let them build you a delightful dwelling,
and may you enjoy yourself with throngs of women.”
“Grant us the opportunity out of favor;
let us both exercise this sovereignty.
“O King, having seen the fruit of misconduct,”
And the great fruit of what is well-performed:
I shall restrain myself alone;
I do not crave for children, cattle, or wealth.
Fifty years are the lifespan of mortals here;
yet that limit is not even reached.
Like a reed cut down, it withers away.
In that state, what joy is there, what play, what delight, or what desire for wealth?
"What use have I for sons or wives, O King?
I am released from bondage.
Thus do I understand."
Death does not spare me;
for one seized by the Ender,
what joy is there, and what pursuit of wealth?
O Lord of Men, the birth of humans as caṇḍālas is the lowest,
the most base of bipeds; it is brought about by their own exceedingly evil deeds.
Formerly we dwelt in the womb of a caṇḍāla woman;
we were caṇḍālas among the Avantīs,
as deer near the Nerañjarā River.
The Ukkusā on the banks of the Nammadā—these are the brahmins and khattiyas here today.
Life is being led away; it is short in duration.
For one brought low by old age there is no refuge;
O Pañcāla, do as I say,
and do not perform deeds that result in suffering.
Life is being led away, its span is short;
for one brought low by old age, there is no refuge.
O Pañcāla, do as I say!
Do not perform deeds that bear painful fruit.
Life is being led away, its span is short;
for one led by old age, there is no refuge.
Do as I say, O Pañcāla;
do not perform deeds that lead to the dust of rebirth.
Life is being led away, and it is short in duration.
Old age destroys the beauty of a man as he grows old;
O Pañcāla, do my bidding now, and do not perform an act that leads to rebirth in hell.
“Truly, this word of yours is the truth,
just as you, O seer, have spoken it;
for there are indeed sensual pleasures before me in manifold forms.”
"O monk, such a birth is ill-fated for one like me.
Like an elephant sunk in the midst of a mire,
though seeing dry land, he is unable to reach it."
Thus, being stuck in the mire of sensual pleasures,
I do not follow the path of a bhikkhu,
just as neither mother nor father [would abandon] their son.
"Instruct me how I might be happy; thus, venerable sir,
instruct me so that I may be happy for a long time after passing away."
“If you, O Lord of Men, are not able to abandon these human sensual pleasures, then,
O King, establish a righteous offering.”
Let there be no injustice in your kingdom.
Let messengers run forth to the four quarters,
inviting śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
Serve them with food and drink,
and with clothing and the requisite of lodgings.
With a mind full of faith, provide them with food and drink.
Satisfy the recluses and brahmins;
having given and eaten according to your means,
go, blameless, to the heavenly realm.
And if, O King, while you are being entertained by throngs of women, that intoxication should overcome you,
then keep this very verse in mind:
He spoke thus in the midst of the assembly:
"A person who has been suckled at the breast and is now walking about sleeps in the open air."
“Surrounded by dogs,
he is today called ‘King’.
Thus ends the second Jātaka, the Cittasambhūta-jātaka.
